analysis.one_liner: Caps carbon emissions from oil, coal, and natural gas and pays the auction proceeds out as equal dividends to every American.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to two House committees and a subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required oil refineries and importers, coal mines, and natural gas suppliers to buy permits for the carbon their fuels emit, with the number of permits shrinking every year until emissions were 80% below 2005 levels by 2050. All the auction money, minus administration costs, would go back to every lawful resident with a Social Security number as an equal quarterly dividend. It also put border fees on carbon-intensive imports and paid matching rebates to exporters, so U.S. manufacturers wouldn't be undercut by countries without carbon rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Every lawful resident with a valid Social Security number would receive an equal share of the permit auction proceeds as a tax-free quarterly dividend; for most households, especially lower- and middle-income ones who use less fuel than average, the dividend would exceed the higher fuel prices the cap creates. Future generations and communities exposed to air pollution would also gain from the steadily declining emissions cap.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All lawful residents with a Social Security number

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs that Healthy Climate Trust Fund amounts not used for administration be paid out as equal quarterly 'Healthy Climate Dividend Payments' to every eligible individual with a valid Social Security number, excluded from gross income so they are not taxed.

The number of carbon permits declines on a fixed schedule to 80% below 2005 emissions levels by 2050, so emissions fall regardless of price fluctuations, and permits carry no property right, letting the government terminate or limit them.

Carbon equivalency fees on carbon-intensive imports, with matching payments to U.S. exporters, keep steel, cement, glass, and other energy-intensive U.S. manufacturers competitive against producers in countries without carbon costs.

Auction rules limit how many permits a single entity can buy or hold to prevent speculation and hoarding, and a penalty of three times the permit price applies to companies that emit without surrendering permits.

analysis.who_pays: Oil refineries and petroleum importers, coal mines, and natural gas suppliers and processors would buy permits for every ton of carbon their fuels emit, costs that would be passed through to consumers in the price of gasoline, electricity, and heating fuel. Households that drive and heat more than average would pay more than their dividend.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and heavy fuel users

drawbacks.text: Permit costs would be passed through to consumers, raising prices for gasoline, home heating, and electricity; households with high fuel use or without easy alternatives could pay more than they receive in dividends.

The bill excludes methane and other emissions from livestock production from its regulatory list, leaving a significant greenhouse gas source to separate Clean Air Act rules that are not specified in the bill.
The cap allows companies to borrow future-year permits when prices spike, and permits can be banked indefinitely, which could delay emissions cuts in some years even as the long-term cap holds.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design puts the burden on the fossil fuels causing the problem and returns the money equally to every person, which by construction favors lower- and middle-income households that emit less than average. The main honest objections are the energy price increases for high-consumption households and industries, and the fact that a price-driven system depends on careful administration to prevent permit-market manipulation. The declining physical cap limits the risk that emissions targets are missed, but not the risk of price volatility.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the House in July 2014, referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, sent to the Energy and Power Subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Van Hollen introduced the bill in the House on July 30, 2014, joined by nine original cosponsors.
It was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and, additionally, to the Committee on Ways and Means, for consideration of the provisions under each committee's jurisdiction.
On August 1, 2014, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the 113th Congress.
The bill had 15 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no recorded committee or floor action of any kind.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers — coal mines, oil refiners, and natural gas suppliers — avoided a new cost on every ton of carbon they sell, because the bill never advanced. No one else gained from its death; the dividends and emissions reductions it promised never materialized.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers avoided the carbon cost

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored its cap-and-dividend structure, requiring permit purchases from fossil fuel producers and equal dividends back to the public.

for.what_they_did: Joined as one of nine original cosponsors at introduction.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 15 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 30, 2014, sent it to the Energy and Power Subcommittee on August 1, and never scheduled a hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received a split referral for the tax provisions and took no recorded action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were House Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; no roll-call votes were ever taken, but the House, under Republican control, gave the bill no committee action beyond a subcommittee referral.

industries.note: Every coal mine and coal importer would have to buy permits for the carbon in the coal it sells, with the permit supply shrinking each year. Passing the cost to electricity customers is why coal interests opposed carbon pricing.

Refineries and petroleum product importers would buy permits for the carbon emitted when their fuels are burned, a direct new cost on every barrel and gallon. This is the industry whose fuel prices rise under the cap.
Gas suppliers and processors would face the same permit obligation, raising the cost of a fuel many households use for heating. Like oil and coal, the industry's interest ran against the bill.

industries.industry: Energy-intensive manufacturers (steel, cement, glass, chemicals, paper)
industries.note: The bill raises their production costs through permit prices on fuel, but border adjustment fees on comparable imports and rebates to exporters are designed to leave them on roughly equal footing with foreign competitors.
